repos.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
repos.paper_summary: Harness2 is a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing. It refines an LLM agent's execution harness (its prompts, memory, skills, tools, and related components) for each task, and it updates a separate improvement harness across tasks. Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step. It proposes harness edits, runs them under matched conditions against a reference execution, and composes only changes supported by behavioral contrasts, without a ground-truth verifier. Parallel recursion composes from a pool of candidates, and sequential recursion chains revisions. Both are controlled by a budget k. After each task, reflection adds adopted harnesses and supported lessons to a library that guides later proposals. On WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB (Partial pass rate), with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex, one step improves every configuration by up to 11.5 points, 4.5 points, and 11.8 percentage points. Parallel recursion at k=5 adds up to 3.9, 4.2, and 6.7 more. The authors state that probe contrasts are limited by execution stochasticity and shared model biases, and that adopted harnesses are not verified to be optimal.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 targets open-world agent harness evolution, which lacks ground-truth verifiers and fails to transfer across tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness2
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 pairs task-level recursion, which refines the current harness without verifiers, with a library that carries lessons to later tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Single-step Harness2 exceeds the base harness on all three benchmarks for GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under both initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Score gains grow with recursion budget, and each ablated component lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 differs from prior harness optimization by learning from its own refinements across a task stream without ground-truth feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Harness2 turns task-specific refinement into reusable experience, with gains reported across three benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers comparison criteria, benchmark splits, baselines, tool-call errors, production harness comparison, failure cases, limitations, and prompts.

repos.title: Attention Is All You Need
repos.paper_summary:
The Transformer is a sequence transduction model that replaces recurrent and convolutional layers with multi-head self-attention. The architecture consists of six encoder and six decoder stacks, each containing sub-layers for scaled dot-product attention and position-wise feed-forward networks. Positional information is injected via fixed sinusoidal encodings added to token embeddings.

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the large variant achieves 28.4 BLEU, exceeding previous best ensembles by over 2.0 BLEU. For English-to-French, it reaches 41.8 BLEU after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs. A base configuration requires only 12 hours of training on the same hardware. The model also generalizes to English constituency parsing, achieving 92.7 F1 in a semi-supervised setting. Limitations include quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length and reliance on beam search during inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Recurrent models process positions sequentially, which limits parallelization; the authors propose the Transformer, which uses only attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior convolutional models need operations that grow with distance between positions; the Transformer reduces this to a constant number.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: The model stacks six encoder and decoder layers built on scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, with sinusoidal positional encodings.

digest_headlines.heading: Why Self-Attention
digest_headlines.headline: Self-attention needs a constant number of sequential operations and a constant maximum path length, versus linear for recurrent layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Models trained on WMT 2014 data with Adam and a warmup learning-rate schedule, using dropout and label smoothing.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: The big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, above prior results including ensembles, and generalizes to parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the Transformer trains faster than recurrent or convolutional models and plan to extend it to other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix shows layer-5 encoder attention heads tracking long-distance verb dependencies, anaphora, and sentence structure.

repos.title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
repos.paper_summary: DeepTutor is an open-source agentic tutoring framework that combines citation-grounded problem tutoring with difficulty-calibrated question generation, both driven by a shared learner model. Its Hybrid Personalization Engine pairs Static Knowledge Grounding (knowledge-graph traversal plus dense search, fused by reciprocal rank fusion) with Dynamic Personal Memory, a trace forest of past interactions. Three memory agents query this forest and update a learner profile after each session. Tutoring proceeds through investigation, guided solving, and evidence-based writing. Question generation selects ideas, then a separate validator checks each question, answer, and explanation. TutorBench covers five university-level disciplines, with learner profiles tied to course material and evaluated by an LLM student simulator and rubric-based assessors. DeepTutor improves personalized metrics by 10.8% on average, and a solver-only transfer study shows a 29.4% average gain across five backbone models. Human raters and the LLM judge show aligned preference trends. Stated limitations include simulated rather than real learners, no large-scale human student study, and added inference cost. The Book Engine and Partners are described architecturally without learner-outcome evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing tutoring and question-generation workflows run in isolation, so tutoring traces do not shape later practice items.

digest_headlines.heading: DeepTutor Framework
digest_headlines.headline: A shared personalization engine feeds problem tutoring and question generation, and every completed interaction updates the learner profile.

digest_headlines.heading: Extending the Personalization Substrate
digest_headlines.headline: Extensions such as Deep Research, Mastery Path and the Book Engine reuse one personalization substrate, while quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core.

digest_headlines.heading: TutorBench
digest_headlines.headline: TutorBench pairs 90 learner profiles from 30 knowledge bases in five disciplines with 270 source-grounded interactive tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor reaches 3.91 overall quality on TutorBench against 3.53 for the Naive Tutor baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers LLM memory, knowledge tracing and LLM tutors, and finds adaptive tutoring on individualized materials underexplored.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: DeepTutor improves overall quality by 10.8% on TutorBench and yields a 29.4% average gain across five backbone families.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive results rest on LLM simulators and rubric judges, and the extensions' effects on real learners remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extended related work, implementation details, TutorBench construction, evaluation protocol, hyperparameters and backbone models.

repos.title: ResearchStudio-Reel: Automate the Last Mile of Research from Paper to Poster, Video, and Blog
repos.paper_summary:
ResearchStudio-Reel is a set of five skills, runnable in Claude Code and Codex, that turns one paper PDF into an editable PowerPoint poster, a narrated talk video with a PowerPoint deck, and a bilingual Word blog. A shared extractor, Paper2Assets, builds one bundle of text, cleaned figures, metadata, and section IDs that all three generators read, so none of them re-parses the PDF. Paper2Poster uses a measured-fill loop that scores each section's fill ratio, edits sections until they fall between 0.90 and 0.98, and requires figures to fill at least 90% of their card. Paper2Reel then links poster regions, video segments, and blog passages in one HTML viewer.

On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, the Claude Code configuration has the best scores among automated systems on all three aesthetic sub-criteria and the best or tied-best on two of three information sub-criteria. Under two VLM judges, its average aesthetic score is 3.56 versus 3.03 for the authors' posters, and it wins overall on 74 and 95 of the 100 papers.

The paper states that its evaluative, generative, and architectural limits remain to be studied. The provided text reports no quantitative evaluation for the video or blog artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paper-to-poster, video, and blog tools mostly stay artifact-specific, so the paper proposes an editable, linked workspace for all three.

digest_headlines.heading: Skills
digest_headlines.headline: Five skills share one extracted bundle, with three generators feeding a single interactive viewer that keeps sections aligned.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 100-paper benchmark, the Claude Code configuration scores 3.56 on aesthetics against the authors' 3.03.

digest_headlines.heading: Applications
digest_headlines.headline: Three intended users, an individual author, a lab, and a course, would run the same pipeline at different cadences.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior paper-to-poster, video, and blog systems each target one output, while this work binds editable artifacts into one linked viewer.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation relies on proxy measures, and the pipeline cannot yet create new method or overview diagrams.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Editable, linked artifacts are delivered, with posters above the authors' own on aesthetics under two judges.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists failure modes, scope limits, ethics, reproducibility, per-judge scores, comparisons, a gallery, and the baseline prompt.

repos.title: CAVEWOMAN: How Large Language Models Behave Under Linguistic Input and Output Compression
repos.paper_summary:
Cavewoman is a two-channel evaluation protocol that measures task accuracy, realized per-item cost, and reference-text agreement for large language models under linguistic compression. The method applies deterministic part-of-speech filters to user prompts (input compression) or constrains model responses via system prompts (output compression) across five reduction levels. It evaluates eight models on five datasets, including GSM8K and MMLU-STEM, totaling 11,465 items per model.

Output compression reduces realized cost by 1.4–2.4× on most API models and up to 3× in the best case, while input compression increases net cost by approximately 1.15× on average due to compensatory output expansion. Under output compression, 51.9% of generations from non-reasoning models are correct but their surface text no longer entails the model’s unconstrained baseline; this rate rises to 80.4% under length-controlled re-scoring. The paper notes that robustness to compression varies widely across models and is not predicted by parameter count or unconstrained accuracy. Limitations include the use of greedy decoding only, short structured answers that may not generalize to long-form generation, and the fact that NLI judges measure surface-text divergence rather than propositional content.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Accuracy at a reduced token count cannot separate realized cost from prompt reduction, so Cavewoman scores both channels on three axes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior compression methods each reduce one channel and report accuracy at a token budget, and none checks reference-text agreement.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Cavewoman holds the model and question fixed and applies five reduction levels to either the prompt or the response.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Output compression lowers realized cost on most API models while input compression raises it, and correct answers still diverge from reference text.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Single-axis evaluation is underdetermined, because cost, accuracy and reference agreement dissociate and a composite metric can mis-rank methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Candidates should be ranked at their deployment constraint level, since output-compression tolerance is not predicted by parameter count or unconstrained accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists pricing, dataset statistics, inference configuration, token and cost accounting, constraint specifications, and released artifacts.

repos.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
repos.paper_summary: TokenEconomizer is an external controller that reduces token costs for black-box coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI) over sequences of tasks within the same repository, without modifying model weights or agent code. It applies three meta-strategies whose policies are learned from completed traces: activating repository-specific micro-skills, pruning loaded tools that are never called, and intervening in failure loops using a turn budget set from successful prior runs, with an LLM judge deciding whether to redirect or stop. Evaluation covers 277 SWE-Bench tasks across six repositories in five agent–model settings, plus 102 Web-Bench tasks and 200 security-auditing tasks. On SWE-Bench, mean cache-aware cost falls by 18.4–30.9% including controller overhead, and Pass@1 rises in four of five settings; the one drop is 1.0 percentage point on Opus 4.8. Reduced reasoning effort lowers Pass@1 by 1.8–10.3 points in comparison. On Web-Bench and the security benchmarks, cost falls by 16.0–21.2% and 6.4–19.6%, with Pass@2 and detection F1 comparable to default. Limitations: the controller can make incorrect decisions (stale skills, wrongly pruned tools, mistaken loop detection), and SWE-Bench task streams are independent fixes rather than real user sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Recurring coding-agent costs in shared repositories motivate an external controller that learns from completed tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Cost Profiling and Analysis of Fixed Cost-control Strategies
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed cost-control strategies give mixed results by repository, and traces reveal three sources of removable cost.

digest_headlines.heading: TokenEconomizer
digest_headlines.headline: TokenEconomizer selects micro-skills, tool masks, and turn budgets per repository using confirmation, retirement, and failure-loop rules learned from traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the software-engineering benchmark, TokenEconomizer cuts mean cost 18.4–30.9% across five settings, raising Pass@1 in four.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing agent cost methods are typically fixed and task-local, whereas TokenEconomizer adapts cost control from completed traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stale skills, wrongly pruned tools, and mistaken loop detections remain possible, and streams are not real user sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers extended discussion, cost-profiling protocol, controller configuration, task selection, examples, and harness customization.

repos.title: TokenPilot: Cache-Efficient Context Management for LLM Agents
repos.paper_summary:
TokenPilot is a context management framework for LLM agents that reduces inference costs by aligning text compression with prompt cache continuity. It operates at two granularities: Ingestion-Aware Compaction stabilizes the prompt prefix by replacing volatile runtime variables with static placeholders and stripping structural noise from tool responses before they enter the context window; Lifecycle-Aware Eviction monitors context segments in batches, offloading them only when their estimated residual utility expires. This prevents the layout mutations that typically invalidate hardware KV caches.

Evaluated on PinchBench (123 tasks) and Claw-Eval (161 tasks) using GPT-5.4-mini, TokenPilot reduces total inference cost by 61% and 56% in isolated mode, and 61% and 87% in continuous mode, respectively, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. For instance, on Claw-Eval continuous mode, it lowers cost from USD 81.52 to USD 10.58. The system requires backend support for prefix caching and relies on a model-based estimator that may misclassify segments under ambiguous interaction patterns. Additionally, performance gains depend on grouping same-category tasks into contiguous sessions, as heterogeneous streams exhibit lower prefix reuse rates due to frequent tool schema changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Text pruning cuts tokens but mutates prompt layouts and breaks cache reuse, so TokenPilot pairs ingestion stabilization with lifecycle eviction.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Serving cost is modeled as discounted cache-hit tokens plus full-cost miss tokens across isolated and continuous task modes.

digest_headlines.heading: TokenPilot
digest_headlines.headline: The framework stabilizes prompt prefixes at ingestion and evicts context segments only after their residual utility expires, in batches of turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On Claw-Eval isolated mode, TokenPilot scores 63.1 at USD 2.27 cost, versus Vanilla's 64.5 at USD 5.16.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers static text compression, passive memory retrieval and summarization, and runtime paging and scheduling of context.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion states that TokenPilot cuts inference cost in both modes without sacrificing task effectiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include estimator misclassification, tuning of threshold tau and batch size, dependence on prefix caching, and weaker reuse on shuffled streams.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark statistics, cost formula and prices, baseline settings, hyperparameters, estimator prompts, and mixed-category results.

repos.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
repos.paper_summary: Edge0 is a streaming inference engine for 35B-class mixture-of-experts models on a 24 GB consumer machine. Expert weights stay on SSD and are memory-mapped on demand, so peak memory tracks the active experts, not all parameters. A per-layer prerouter head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so expert reads overlap the current forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing itself, so the staged experts match the routed experts and none are dropped. An unmerged int4 recovery LoRA, distilled from the fp16 teacher on the student routing path, recovers quality lost to quantization and routing replacement. On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB, the 35B tier decodes at 20.4 tok/s with 2.9 GiB peak active memory, and the 8B tier at 28.0 tok/s with 1.5 GiB. On OpenCompass, the 35B tier averages 79.2 against 83.2 for its fp16 base, and the 8B tier 69.9 against 72.7. Limitations: AIME loses 6.1 points (35B) and 10.0 points (8B), requests are served one at a time, and CPU graph building sets a 44 ms per-step floor.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.

repos.title: Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research Agents
repos.paper_summary: Scientific Agent Skills is an open library of 163 procedural skills for research agents, spanning 16 areas including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned Markdown instruction file, often with reference documents and scripts. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it. The paper is a resource description. It reports no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. It measures two corpus properties at tag v2.65.0. The always-resident descriptions of all skills cost 7.1% of a 200,000-token window. The median of the 46 documented workflows fits within 23.9% of that window, although 29 of the 46 would overflow if every reference file were loaded. Lexical analysis finds a median nearest-neighbour cosine similarity of 0.15 between descriptions, with the closest pair at 0.40. Limitations include no evidence that skills improve agent outcomes, no measured selection accuracy, and uneven review, since 32 of 163 skills do not list the maintainers as author.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agents often return working code that is not defensible, so the paper proposes a library of field-specific procedures packaged as agent skills.

digest_headlines.heading: What an agent skill is
digest_headlines.headline: Each skill is a directory whose instruction file is read only when relevant, keeping most documentation out of standing context.

digest_headlines.heading: What the library covers
digest_headlines.headline: The library's 163 skills cover 16 self-assigned categories, most shipping reference documents, and the workflows combine them unevenly.

digest_headlines.heading: Can descriptions distinguish among skills?
digest_headlines.headline: Most skill descriptions are lexically well separated, but a few neighbouring pairs remain close and some lack authored guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Do the skills a workflow needs fit in context?
digest_headlines.headline: Documented workflows fit a 200,000-token window in their instruction files, but 29 of 46 overflow if every reference file loads.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The paper reports no task-level evaluation, measures selection only as a lexical proxy, and does not test host portability.

digest_headlines.heading: Availability and citation
digest_headlines.headline: Work using the library should cite the paper and tag v2.65.0, and name each skill's metadata version.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendices list the tokenizer and token ledger, skill contents, category counts, routing sensitivity and installed-base estimate.

repos.title: When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
repos.paper_summary: This paper analyzes marginal utility in LLM test-time compute scaling, identifying that extended reasoning often degrades performance through "overthinking." The authors define a flip ratio to track when models abandon correct answers for incorrect ones as token budgets increase. Using DeepSeek-R1-32B and s1-32B on AIME 2024/2025, MATH-500, and GPQA Diamond, they measure accuracy across reasoning budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens via budget forcing. Results show marginal utility turns negative beyond 12K tokens, with the flip ratio exceeding 1.0 at approximately 7K tokens, indicating net harm from additional thinking. Easy problems (Level 1–2) exhibit overthinking at 2K tokens, while hard problems benefit up to 8K. A cost-aware evaluation framework using a tunable $\lambda$ parameter demonstrates that stopping at moderate budgets reduces computation by 50% with only 6% accuracy loss compared to peak performance. Limitations include the focus on mathematical and scientific reasoning tasks and the use of forced continuations, though natural long-reasoning samples confirm similar degradation patterns.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper tests whether more reasoning tokens keep improving accuracy and tracks answers that flip from correct to incorrect.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work reports accuracy gains with compute, and some concurrent studies document overthinking, but few measure marginal returns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Compute is measured in reasoning tokens, using budget forcing, with marginal utility, flip events, and overthinking indicators defined.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Two 32B models show accuracy peaking near 12K tokens and flip ratios above 1 from about 7K tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Cost-Aware Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Cost-weighted scoring favors stopping near 6K tokens, which yields about 50% compute reduction for about 6% accuracy loss.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Marginal utility falls at high budgets and models overthink, so the authors urge reporting efficiency frontiers alongside accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only math and science tasks and open-weight models, and causal mechanisms of overthinking remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The authors argue that identifying wasted extra computation can reduce energy use and emissions from language model inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers how natural long-reasoning samples were selected, their accuracy by output length, and their reconsideration patterns.
